When the Canadian government earlier this year shut down its independent watchdog responsible for investigating alleged human rights abuses including environmental pollution by Canada-based companies operating overseas, it promised that a little-known office called the National Contact Point would take over that work. Two months into Mark Carney’s tenure as Canada’s prime minister, the position became vacant. Carney never appointed a new ombudsperson. The man in the Zambian prison recalled how he ended up there. He’d been approached by someone who had an uncle in the capital, Lusaka, who was willing to buy ivory and pangolin scales. He gave the man a phone and a number to reach him. “He promised that the money I would get would enable me to build a house and take my children to school,” the man said. The story of this inmate — who was eventually arrested and incarcerated for an elephant-related offense — drives home an important truth. Wildlife crime is a multifaceted industry fueled by various participants with a slew of motives, ranging from local people who may occasionally capture and sell an animal to middlemen who handle logistics to heavily armed poaching gangs and the kingpins that rule over large international syndicates. Now, the charity is launching a new award for railway stations to honour the volunteers who keep platforms planted with cheerful flowers and pretty shrubs. Five of the best have been shortlisted for the RHS Railway Stations in Bloom competition, marked for their beauty but also for how well they welcome wildlife and withstand changing climate conditions. Also from Essex, she managed to grow plants in dry ground that had never been cultivated. “It’s transformed the centre of the village,” said the lead volunteer, Frank Belgrave. Ten years ago the station was described in the local paper as “rundown”. Now, the planting beds rival any at Chelsea flower show. Belgrave said residents were very pleased their station had received the spruce-up: “It’s wonderful. People sometimes stop by with plants and compost to help us, and we are very lucky to have some lovely volunteers as the garden requires constant maintenance. “We used to spend all our time watering. cards.source_text: Summer is at an end, and suddenly spiders seem to be everywhere – in your house, in your garden, in your hair. Fresh webs hang from doorways, walls, shrubs and fence posts, creating invisible obstacle courses. Where do all these spiders come from, what kind are they and what, if anything, should we do about them? The short answer to the question “Why are there so many more spiders at this time of year?” is: there aren’t. They are just more obvious. Dave Clarke, an ectotherm (“cold-blooded” animal) specialist at the Zoological Society of London, says: “There are more spiders around in the spring, because that’s when they hatch from their egg sacs, and there are hundreds of babies in each egg sac. But they’re small and not very obvious. They grow up during the summer and, at this time of year, they reach their maximum size.” Their webs are also correspondingly larger. The other reason they are more apparent is that they are finding their way indoors in the desperate search for a mate. Dr Sara Goodacre, professor of evolutionary biology and genetics at the University of Nottingham, says: “The ones you see in your home at the minute, the really big, fat, hairy ones, they’re usually teenage males that are lost – emotionally, geographically – and are just hoping they might find a female so they can continue the life cycle.” The spider season can be a difficult time for people who don’t like spiders, but a little knowledge about these fascinating creatures can go a long way to promote understanding. Here, then, are the 10 spiders you’re most likely to run into this autumn. 1. House spider (Tegenaria domestica) One of the species you are likely to find in your home, the house spider ranges from pale to dark brown, with black markings and banded, hairy legs. While the name seems to imply that it thrives only within four walls, that is not the case. “They’re not called house spiders because they have to live in your house,” says Clarke. “It’s just because it’s the commonest species you would see inside the house.” Centrally heated homes are generally too dry and too short of food for most species of spider so you don’t have to feel bad about gently relocating one. “It’s your home,” says Goodacre. “You decide who you share it with.” If you wish to evict a house spider, trap it gently in an upturned glass and slide a piece of card underneath the glass. He learned it from older monks who came before him, who learned it in turn in an unbroken chain stretching back to Athanasios the Athonite, in AD963. Over the centuries, individual monks have come and gone, and yet their chants, prayers, oaths, costumes and ceremonies endure. This persistence is remarkable and revealing: cultural traditions endure because they share a fundamental property with biological organisms. They are alive. Not metaphorically, but literally. I believe that human culture isn’t just an accidental add-on to organic life; rather, it’s a separate expression of life in its own right. But first we should define our terms. What is life? There isn’t just one answer; indeed, the lack of a clear definition has become a kind of bad joke among life scientists, who can’t quite agree what it is they actually study. One attribute of life that most biologists would say is critical, however, is the encoding, processing and transmission of information. In organic life, this is the function of genes. Information about how to survive and reproduce is written in DNA, processed by cells and transmitted over generations. Thanks to occasional copying errors and the sifting of natural selection, biological information has evolved to produce the extraordinary diversity of life on Earth today. But millions of years ago, a second kind of self-perpetuating information appeared – one that wasn’t written in DNA or read by cells, but which nonetheless began to replicate and propagate itself through time. And it has evolved and diversified to create the stupefying complexity of the modern world. We call it culture. Cultures consist of knowledge or behaviours transmitted from one individual to another through social learning. We used to believe culture was uniquely human, but animals have cultures, too. Chimpanzees from some parts of west Africa use rocks to crack nuts, for example, but in other parts they don’t, even though the same nuts and rocks are available; in some places they strip sticks of their leaves to fish termites from their nests; and elsewhere they use moss as a sponge from which to drink water. There had been an attempted film adaptation before that, but he had been unsurprised by its failure, having warned that it was impossible to condense his densely plotted doorstopper of a novel into a feature-length film. This time, Franzen had signed up as co-writer, with filmmaker Noah Baumbach. He says that HBO was “excluded from the development process. Mistake, because we didn’t know how to do TV.” Franzen himself hadn’t even owned a telly until a few years earlier and certainly didn’t have cable, so as he was wrestling with the script, he began renting box sets. Around three episodes into one drama series, he realised “we have no idea what we’re doing. This is not how you do TV. This is bad,” he recalls. The result, he says, was “one of the worst pilots anyone has ever made”. Franzen used to think TV was the “enemy” of the serious novelist. In a well-known 1996 essay for Harper’s Magazine about the decline of high literature he had complained bitterly about the “banal ascendancy of television”. But after the HBO series failed, he watched Breaking Bad, Nurse Jackie and Silicon Valley and loved them. In the age of social media, AI and the endless scroll, TV has started to look like a “friend”, he says now. And The Corrections is finally being adapted into an eight-part Netflix series, with Meryl Streep playing Enid Lambert, the matriarch clinging to dreams of hosting a perfect last family Christmas, even as her husband Alfred is in terminal decline with Parkinson’s and dementia and their grownup children’s lives are falling apart in terrible, comical ways. cards.source_text: You may have heard her songs, seen her videos, maybe even attended one of her concerts … but have you seen the new genus of Australian plant bugs named after Taylor Swift? Scientists at the University of California, Riverside recently described a new genus of plant bugs, they’ve named Swiftiephylus, in honor of the Grammy-winning U.S. singer. The genus contains 12 new species of plant bugs. Four of the insects are named after Taylor Swift or her albums: Swiftiephylus taylorae, Swiftiephylus amator, Swiftiephylus intrepidus, and Swiftiephylus poetorum. The first is a Latinized version of Taylor; the others are references to her albums “Lover,” “Fearless” and “The Tortured Poets Department.” The authors write that the insects were named after Taylor Swift, “in recognition of her show-stopping talent, heart-wrenching lyrics, and the joy and comfort she has brought to many. The term ‘Swifitie’ refers to Swift’s loving fanbase,” the study notes. Study author and “Swiftie” Sarah Schroeder said in a press release that she named the insects after Taylor Swift’s appearance. “Taylor Swift’s iconic look is her blonde hair and red lips. These insects are pale yellow with accents of red throughout,” Schroeder said. “In the paper I refer to them as blonde.” Schroeder believes that their coloring helps the bugs camouflage in the flowers they live on, which feature spindly red to orange flowers. Though many species of insects are broadly called bugs, Swiftiephylus plant bugs are part of the Miridae family, the largest family of true bugs. There are more than 11,000 described species of true bugs in the Miridae family worldwide. The bugs in this study were collected between 1995 and 2004 and borrowed from museum collections to be formally described. Swiftiephylus plant bugs feed on trees and shrubs in Australia, though they are relatively harmless to their host plants and aren’t known agricultural pests. Unlike their namesake, the Swiftiephylus are silent bugs and have no known musical talent. cards.source_text: When I was asked to write the first full-length Miss Marple novel since Sleeping Murder was published posthumously, 50 years ago in October, I immediately thought of my granny. My first encounter with the world of Agatha Christie was through her. Now I come to think of it, she was a rather Marple-ish figure in many ways: a keen knitter and gardener with a brilliant mind (she could complete the “big” crossword in seemingly about 15 minutes), highly perceptive about people and human nature and with a powerful moral compass. While kind and generous beyond measure, at times, like Miss Marple, she showed a steelier side. Christie created Jane Marple in a Christmas magazine story called The Tuesday Night Club in 1927, and this “white-haired old lady” made her book debut in 1930 with The Murder at the Vicarage. Rivalling Hercule Poirot in her readers’ affections, Miss Marple eventually appeared in 12 of the author’s 66 detective novels, plus 20 of her 160 short stories. With more than 1bn Agatha Christie books sold in English, and another 1bn sold in translation, they are some of the most perpetually loved works ever written. But though Sophie Hannah was commissioned by Christie’s family to publish an authorised continuation of her Poirot novels in 2013, no one had ever been asked to write a new Miss Marple. Until now … As well as feeling honour, and terror, at the invitation to take up Christie’s beloved character, I had a funny sense of homecoming. Christie has always been so important to me as a reader and writer. Hers was the first adult fiction I read, at around 12 or 13, beginning with Murder on the Orient Express – what a place to start! I’m not sure I was even really aware of the death and darkness there, I was just taken up by the game of it all: trying to spot the clues and dodge the red herrings, to guess the solution before the big reveal. I remember distinctly the experience, that any mystery reader will recognise, of wanting to race through the pages to get to the solution and yet also to eke it all out. I worried: what if this brilliant writer, this plotting magician, hadn’t written anything else? Thankfully, that wasn’t a problem. Like many readers, I was drawn to the Poirot books first. cards.source_text: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a single Carly Rae Jepsen record must be in want of its other half. A year after the Canadian pop star released her breakthrough record, 2015’s E•MO•TION, she returned with E•MO•TION Side B. 2019’s Dedicated received similar treatment. By the time Jepsen released the companion album to 2022’s The Loneliest Time, the “surprise” drop hardly registered. This brand of excess is key to Jepsen’s charm. Here is a singer who’ll repeat the word “really” six times in a row in a song’s chorus, just to make sure you really get the message; who claimed she wrote 200 songs for one 12-track record, then another hundred for her next one. Her latest album, Day and Night, tweaks her formula of abundance slightly, offering—in a CRJ first—a full double album upfront. As its title suggests, the record comprises two distinct themes: sweet, sunny tracks for Day; sleeker, dancier songs for Night. Working with a familiar stable of producers and co-writers, she turns out a sprawling album filled with loose, breezy tracks offset by the occasional pop gem and charming left-field details. No score yet, be the first to add. Day hews mostly to the windswept ballads and disco-inflected pop that Jepsen moved toward on her previous set of records: “After All” and “Something Tragic” are lightly psychedelic, her voice all breathy and urgent; there’s a little chillwave on “Habits of Creatures,” a little folk on “Wild Child.” Night is more strictly synth-pop: “Don’t Leave Me on the Dancefloor” is the cleanest ABBA homage she’s ever managed, and I wouldn’t have been surprised to hear the ultra-yearning “That’s Just Me” as a deep-cut E•MO•TION castoff. Day and Night’s sprawl is a double-edged sword. Though the production is usually layered and finely detailed, most songs don’t contain the razor-sharp hooks that usually make Jepsen’s work so indelible. In their absence, each side becomes a little unwieldy, and both Day and Night sag in their second halves. Only a fool would doubt that the prolific Jepsen could write 24 full tracks for a vaguely conceptual double album—but one wonders if a more focused, refined concept would better sustain its momentum. But perhaps a pared-back version of this record wouldn’t allow for the strange, quasi-experimental detours that populate it. Imitate his moody, mewing Canadian whine; adopt his verité approach to studio recording; tune your acoustic guitar to drop-D and overdrive your electric through a vintage amp; rip a solo that’s just one note and dig into the fretboard as if a weaker player handed you their instrument to help wear in the neck. But who else can conjure this kind of grainy, autumnal dream state with such effortlessness and patience, using such spare tools? For the first time since 2012’s louder and gnarlier Psychedelic Pill, Young spends his 50th studio album luxuriating in this gift, casting a glow of bittersweet contentment that feels distinct in his catalog. You could be forgiven for keeping your expectations low. These days, the 80-year-old songwriter’s attention seems largely dominated by his Archives project—the type of comprehensive legacy curation that tends to be handed off entirely to the label but which Young has continued to operate in a charmingly messy state of constant, unpredictable motion. Along the way, his new records, more than ever, seem to exist mainly to document passing obsessions, feelings, and company. From a trio of understated Crazy Horse reunion records between 2019 and 2022 to last year’s wispy and unsteady Talkin to the Trees—the debut of his new backing band, the Chrome Hearts—these statements are always welcome but rarely essential. No score yet, be the first to add. Upon entering the studio earlier this year, even Young wasn’t sure about his latest crop of material, confessing to Archives subscribers that he “ran out of tunes fast.” Really, he just had five songs—and “songs” might even be stretching it. These were slow, formless meditations, several hovering around the 10-minute mark, ambling along to breezy, familiar chord changes on acoustic guitar and piano. cards.source_text: The story could scarcely be more simple: two committed patriots off to find America. The iconic, oft-referenced sequence in 1969’s psychedelic biker opera Easy Rider features the film’s twinned anti-heroes, Billy and Wyatt, tearing down a sprawling U.S. highway astride two choppers at some impossible speed, soundtracked by one of the greatest badass statements of purpose rock’n’roll ever yielded: Steppenwolf’s “Born to Be Wild.” It’s a song that perfectly bisects the dueling hippie impulses between the communitarian and utopian, and the hedonistically self-fascinated, a painful cleavage which was coming to the fore just as Easy Rider hit screens in July 1969. Can you picture it? Set against the monster rock riffs of lead guitarist Michael Monarch, singer John Kay’s edict to “take the world in a love embrace” sits nervously alongside the tune’s insinuating thirst for danger: “I like smoke and lightning/Heavy metal thunder.” This is the dichotomy that would define both the film and the soundtrack, the pastoral, pacific drop-out resistance of the Summer of Love running directly into the fraught entropy of an ersatz movement losing steam and beginning to cannibalize itself. It’s an image of such pure lawless liberation, from blue-to-red-state America, I’m not sure we’ve ever fully recovered. It’s way more “don’t tread on me” than “come on people now, smile on your brother.” In my mind—and I’ve seen the movie many, many times—I always think this is how Easy Rider starts. No score yet, be the first to add. The actual first scene in Easy Rider is intensely uneasy, a tenuous south-of-the-border drug deal that has all the hallmarks of a classic Treasure of the Sierra Madre-style misunderstanding. But no. Peter Fonda and Dennis Hopper—the film’s titular motorcycle muses—manage to fence what looks like a bumper crop of coke to a louche-looking drug connect played by Phil Spector, who sends them off with generational cash in exchange. cards.source_text: Last year, the fashion writer Biz Sherbert went to a Deftones concert in Atlanta and interviewed attendees before the show. The 2020s revitalization of the alt-metal pioneers is pretty well established at this point, but Sherbert’s documentation showed off the band’s popularity with young women specifically; she photographed teenagers and college students in miniskirts and tank tops, many of whom had discovered Deftones algorithmically, through Spotify or TikTok. The scene looked a lot different than the one I remember from seeing the band in 2003 in a sea of black-clad nu-metal bros. One group of young women even called Deftones a “girl band,” exclaiming, “This is girly pop music!” So when Deftones vocalist Chino Moreno shows up to do backing vocals for the last track of Beabadoobee’s latest album, it makes all the sense in the world, Beatrice Laus, currently 26 years old, has made her share of music that could be called “girly pop,” but with her fourth studio album, Pylon, she threads the needle between her usual brand of sweet-but-melancholic pop rock, and a newer, rougher sound. The ingredients that gave 2024’s This Is How Tomorrow Moves its darling tweeness—peppy horns, tender piano—have been replaced with elements that will please anyone who spent their adolescence learning how to professionally glower: tapped harmonics, twirly twin guitar loops, sludgy riffs, screeching feedback. It’s a reverse Sour Patch Kid situation—first Beabadoobee was sweet, now she’s getting sour. No score yet, be the first to add. To solidify the vibe shift, Laus has tapped an impressive breadth of alt-rock stars from the past couple of decades. Besides Moreno, we get vocals from Hayley Williams, guitar and songwriting contributions from Title Fight’s Shane Moran, one song co-written with Evan Stephens Hall from Pinegrove (one of Laus’s favorite bands, to the point of her getting a Pinegrove neck tattoo last year), and an appearance from Turnstile’s Brendan Yates so dour that, at first listen, I thought he was Bladee. The guestlist is stacked, but nothing on the album sounds particularly like Pinegrove or Deftones or Title Fight (Paramore is maybe the closest comp). Rather, the guests seem like they’re here to gently cheer on the grunge-ification of typical Beabadoobee mode: easily digestible lyrics about the turbulent emotions of young adulthood with sticky, straightforward melodies. cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 20 minute listen It is 9 am on a warm July Sunday in Cambridge, as I head towards a café in the city centre. The bells of Great St Mary’s church play the familiar melody of the Cambridge Quarters. The sound, now often associated with the chimes of Big Ben in London, was first composed here in 1793. The quarters, named for the melody at each quarter-hour, are an immediately recognisable reminder of the passage of time. Each bell produces a note: a wave with a characteristic frequency that travels through the air and reaches our ears. A hammer strikes the bell, and it oscillates, pushing air molecules back and forth. Those jostling molecules reach our ears and we hear a musical note. Then the bell settles, gives up its energy, and returns to silence. My research here at the University of Cambridge often brings me back to the ringing of a bell. I don’t study the physics of sound, but I do focus on a remarkably similar process, taking place throughout the Universe. I am interested in another object that also rings: a black hole. As I sit down with a coffee, I open my laptop to a wavy signal that gradually fades to a flat line. Two black holes have finished merging – a frenzied process of coalescence – leaving an extremely brief wiggle originating from the remnant black hole. Much like the struck bell, this leftover black hole is ringing in a process called ringdown, and it’s consistent across every merger I investigate. Ringdown allows physicists to test their theories of gravity: did Albert Einstein really have the last word? Just as an off-sounding note from a bell might indicate a design flaw, a discrepancy in the frequencies of a ringing black hole could be the first crack in our understanding of gravity. That’s the scientific rationale for studying ringdown, but what fascinates me equally is what happens next. After the black hole rings, it settles into silence. In that moment, lasting only a few milliseconds, the power and intensity of the merger are lost. From the exterior, almost all of that history suddenly becomes inaccessible, and what is left is featureless. The black hole settles into a simple, peaceful object of pure spacetime, with no trace of the violence that just happened. In some respects, the black holes forget. It seems counterintuitive that something so chaotically created can become so simple. Why do black holes seem to forget their violent histories? The room was packed full of appliances, as if a commercial kitchen had been blown apart. Several stacks of wall ovens huddled together on dollies. Tangles of electrical cords popped up behind a broad stainless-steel counter. Rags and sponges dried slowly on the edge of a giant sink, over which a pre-rinse nozzle drooped like a willow branch. Nearby, a computer monitor showed Python developer tools next to a spreadsheet dotted with red and green cells. In the middle of the room was an improvised prep station on which there was an odd little machine. It looked like a tiny microwave designed to warm up a single cupcake. I later learned it’s a moisture analyser: the researchers use it to see how much juice is left in their samples of lamb, swordfish, chicken, pork and beef. I’m writing down everything I see: 10:45 am. The kitchen is full of smoke. That basement room was a test kitchen, where two chefs and several researchers had been busy cooking a whole farm’s worth of meat in a set of prototype ovens. The company’s vision was to invent a cooking machine that could whip up Michelin-grade dishes at the press of a button, and the crew was tasting the food and filling out ‘sensory inventory’ forms that recorded qualities like colour, smell, temperature, texture and taste. As the design lead for the oven’s touchscreen interface, I was there to learn from the chefs in order to build something that worked for them and for the ‘home chef’ or end user. The tension between their culinary intuition and the ovens’ logic was immediately apparent: the kitchen was full of smoke because one chef had attempted to cook three racks of lamb directly under a broiler to get the colour you’d get by ‘smacking it with a propane torch’. This instinct didn’t translate to a language the oven understood. I wrote down Smacking? and kept watching. The other chef, tapping away on another of the ovens’ screens, muttered: ‘These things are worthless. I need to be able to use my chef spidey senses.’ The chefs were hired to help program the ovens to follow their recipes. cards.source_text: To what extent can we ever understand the experiences of nonhuman animals? And to what extent do we even understand our own? These questions sit at the heart of the short poetic documentary Animal Eye, which probes the diverse visual worlds of creatures big and small. For the film, the US director Carlo Nasisse pairs the reflections of philosophers and scientists with ruminative in-the-lab images of a wide range of animals. Starting from the biology, beauty and mystery of the eye, Nasisse constructs a broader exploration of the limits of human understanding, and our drive to keep looking regardless. cards.source_text: After the pandemic hit, aspiring indie-pop phenoms seemed to gravitate towards a few common moves: record a couple of covers of Phoebe Bridgers’ Punisher to build an audience; bare your soul to the TikTok algorithm through confessional lyrics; whisper into the microphone like you’re afraid someone might catch you recording alone in your room. Often, just two out of three of these requirements did the trick. It worked for Gracie Abrams, Olivia Rodrigo, and even briefly for Katie Gregson-MacLeod, of “complex” fame. That formula also helped Lizzy McAlpine—a singer-songwriter from Pennsylvania who first garnered attention on social media while a student at Berklee College of Music, uploading videos from home when the pandemic shut down school. Then, her 2022 ballad “Ceilings” sparked a TikTok trend in which people ran away from the camera and passionately belted out its confessional lyrics. The viral success of “Ceilings” epitomized how McAlpine’s early music felt built for a romantic comedy: first swooning, then devastation in the third act. But for her fourth album, Angel, she takes a more homespun approach. McAlpine sounds less like a heroine of a coming-of-age film than a songwriter at an open mic, testing out material for an audience primed to turn songs into snippets. No score yet, be the first to add. Before her third studio album, Older, McAlpine parted ways with producers Philip Etherington and Ehren Ebbage, who were responsible for some of her early hits and had a more cinematic pop flair. Instead, she began working with a live band, making secular songs reminiscent of contemporary worship music. It’s not necessarily the subject matter of songs like “Spring Into Summer” or “Pushing It Down and Praying”; it’s their swelling arrangements, and the fact that McAlpine has a velvety voice fit for a youth worship leader. She continues that trend on Angel. When she sings of “holy ground” and “sacred spaces” on the album’s lead single “The Light in the Painting,” an organ-laden track that evokes a dew-soaked dawn, you can picture her staring out into the crowd, one hand reaching for the heavens and the other clutching her chest like a Disney heroine. Angel is much more traditionally folk and has little of the glossy production that defined her earlier work. The album is built mostly around tender pianos and twangy guitars with the occasional harmonica and bout of whistling. items.title: I was asked to write a new Miss Marple, so I sent her to the Alps
items.summary: Her last case was 50 years ago, written by Agatha Christie just before she died. Could I really follow in the footsteps of the Queen of Crime? When I was asked to write the first full-length Miss Marple novel since Sleeping Murder was published posthumously, 50 years ago in October, I immediately thought of my granny. My first encounter with the world of Agatha Christie was through her. Now I come to think of it, she was a rather Marple-ish figure in many ways: a keen knitter and gardener with a brilliant mind (she could complete the “big” crossword in seemingly about 15 minutes), highly perceptive about people and human nature and with a powerful moral compass. While kind and generous beyond measure, at times, like Miss Marple, she showed a steelier side. Christie created Jane Marple in a Christmas magazine story called The Tuesday Night Club in 1927, and this “white-haired old lady” made her book debut in 1930 with The Murder at the Vicarage. Rivalling Hercule Poirot in her readers’ affections, Miss Marple eventually appeared in 12 of the author’s 66 detective novels, plus 20 of her 160 short stories. With more than 1bn Agatha Christie books sold in English, and another 1bn sold in translation, they are some of the most perpetually loved works ever written. But though Sophie Hannah was commissioned by Christie’s family to publish an authorised continuation of her Poirot novels in 2013, no one had ever been asked to write a new Miss Marple. items.title: Is culture alive?
items.summary: From Mozart to Madonna, dim sum to doughnuts, Shakespeare to Sartre – not all forms of life need DNA On Mount Athos, in northern Greece, a monk rises before dawn to sing the same office that has been sung on that mountain for more than 1,000 years. He learned it from older monks who came before him, who learned it in turn in an unbroken chain stretching back to Athanasios the Athonite, in AD963. Over the centuries, individual monks have come and gone, and yet their chants, prayers, oaths, costumes and ceremonies endure. This persistence is remarkable and revealing: cultural traditions endure because they share a fundamental property with biological organisms. They are alive. Not metaphorically, but literally. items.title: Jonathan Franzen: ‘It’s still mysterious to me that I was angry for so long’
items.summary: The author of The Corrections talks about a new TV adaptation, the future of reading and why creating new work is ‘horrible’ When HBO dropped its plan to adapt Jonathan Franzen’s bestselling novel The Corrections in 2012, the author was so relieved he says he performed his first and last cartwheel on the lawn of his home in Santa Cruz, California. There had been an attempted film adaptation before that, but he had been unsurprised by its failure, having warned that it was impossible to condense his densely plotted doorstopper of a novel into a feature-length film. This time, Franzen had signed up as co-writer, with filmmaker Noah Baumbach. He says that HBO was “excluded from the development process. Mistake, because we didn’t know how to do TV.” Franzen himself hadn’t even owned a telly until a few years earlier and certainly didn’t have cable, so as he was wrestling with the script, he began renting box sets. Around three episodes into one drama series, he realised “we have no idea what we’re doing. This is not how you do TV. This is bad,” he recalls. The result, he says, was “one of the worst pilots anyone has ever made”. Franzen used to think TV was the “enemy” of the serious novelist. In a well-known 1996 essay for Harper’s Magazine about the decline of high literature he had complained bitterly about the “banal ascendancy of television”. But after the HBO series failed, he watched Breaking Bad, Nurse Jackie and Silicon Valley and loved them. In the age of social media, AI and the endless scroll, TV has started to look like a “friend”, he says now. items.title: Spider season! Ten species you’ll see scuttling across Britain’s carpets and lawns this autumn
items.summary: The world is suddenly full of webs and hairy legs. But why? And what do they belong to? Meet the spiders you’re most likely to encounter, from cardinals to false wolves Summer is at an end, and suddenly spiders seem to be everywhere – in your house, in your garden, in your hair. Fresh webs hang from doorways, walls, shrubs and fence posts, creating invisible obstacle courses. Where do all these spiders come from, what kind are they and what, if anything, should we do about them? The short answer to the question “Why are there so many more spiders at this time of year?” is: there aren’t. They are just more obvious. Dave Clarke, an ectotherm (“cold-blooded” animal) specialist at the Zoological Society of London, says: “There are more spiders around in the spring, because that’s when they hatch from their egg sacs, and there are hundreds of babies in each egg sac. But they’re small and not very obvious. They grow up during the summer and, at this time of year, they reach their maximum size.” Their webs are also correspondingly larger. Continue reading...
